questions.question_text: A $600pF$ capacitor is charged by $200V$ supply. It is then disconnected from the supply and is connected to another uncharged $600pF$ capacitor. Electrostatic energy lost in the process is ____________ $\mu J$
questions.question_html: A $600pF$ capacitor is charged by $200V$ supply. It is then disconnected from the supply and is connected to another uncharged $600pF$ capacitor. Electrostatic energy lost in the process is ____________ $\mu J$
questions.explanation_text: The energy stored in a capacitor can be calculated using the formula: $U=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$ where: (U) is the energy, (C) is the capacitance, (V) is the voltage. Initially, the energy stored in the first capacitor is: $U_{\text{initial}}=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \times 600 \times 10^{-12}\text{F} \times (200\text{V})^{2}=0.012\text{J}=12\mu\text{J}.$ When the charged capacitor is connected to the uncharged capacitor, the charge will distribute equally between them because they have the same capacitance. Therefore, the final voltage across each capacitor is half of the initial voltage, i.e., 100 V. The energy in each capacitor after the redistribution is: $U_{\text{final each}}=\frac{1}{2}C(\frac{V}{2})^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \times 600 \times 10^{-12}\text{F} \times (100\text{V})^{2}=0.003\text{J}=3\mu\text{J}.$ As there are two capacitors, the total final energy is: $U_{\text{final total}}=2 \times U_{\text{final each}}=2 \times 3\mu\text{J}=6\mu\text{J}.$ The energy loss is the difference between the initial energy and the final energy: $\Delta U=U_{\text{initial}}-U_{\text{final total}}=12\mu\text{J}-6\mu\text{J}=6\mu\text{J}.$
questions.explanation_html:
The energy stored in a capacitor can be calculated using the formula:

$U=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$

where:

  • (U) is the energy,
  • (C) is the capacitance,
  • (V) is the voltage.

Initially, the energy stored in the first capacitor is:

$U_{\text{initial}}=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \times 600 \times 10^{-12}\text{F} \times (200\text{V})^{2}=0.012\text{J}=12\mu\text{J}.$

When the charged capacitor is connected to the uncharged capacitor, the charge will distribute equally between them because they have the same capacitance. Therefore, the final voltage across each capacitor is half of the initial voltage, i.e., 100 V.

The energy in each capacitor after the redistribution is:

$U_{\text{final each}}=\frac{1}{2}C(\frac{V}{2})^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \times 600 \times 10^{-12}\text{F} \times (100\text{V})^{2}=0.003\text{J}=3\mu\text{J}.$

As there are two capacitors, the total final energy is:

$U_{\text{final total}}=2 \times U_{\text{final each}}=2 \times 3\mu\text{J}=6\mu\text{J}.$

The energy loss is the difference between the initial energy and the final energy:

$\Delta U=U_{\text{initial}}-U_{\text{final total}}=12\mu\text{J}-6\mu\text{J}=6\mu\text{J}.$

If a metal sheet of thickness $\frac{2d}{3}$ and of the same area as plate is introduced between the plates, the capacitance of the capacitor becomes $C_{2}$ . The ratio $\frac{C_{2}}{C_{1}}$ is
questions.question_html: The distance between two plates of a capacitor is $d$ and its capacitance is $C_{1}$ , when air is the medium between the plates. If a metal sheet of thickness $\frac{2d}{3}$ and of the same area as plate is introduced between the plates, the capacitance of the capacitor becomes $C_{2}$ . The ratio $\frac{C_{2}}{C_{1}}$ is
questions.explanation_text: When a metal sheet of thickness ( $\frac{2d}{3}$ ) is introduced between the plates of a capacitor, it divides the capacitor into two separate capacitors. The metal sheet acts as a new plate in each capacitor, and because the metal is a conductor, it is at the same potential as the plates on either side. The capacitance of the original capacitor with air between the plates is given by: $C_{1}=\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{d}$ where ( $\epsilon_{0}$ ) is the permittivity of free space, ( $A$ ) is the area of one of the plates, and ( $d$ ) is the distance between the plates. When the metal sheet of thickness ( $\frac{2d}{3}$ ) is introduced, the distance between the plates is reduced by ( $\frac{2d}{3}$ ), so the capacitance of each of the new capacitors is: $C^{'}=\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{d-\frac{2d}{3}}$ Simplifying, we get: $C^{'}=\frac{3\epsilon_{0}A}{d}$ Since the two capacitors are in parallel with each other, the total capacitance is: $C_{2}=2C^{'}=2 \times \frac{3\epsilon_{0}A}{d}=3C_{1}$ So the ratio of the capacitances is: $\frac{C_{2}}{C_{1}}=3:1$
questions.explanation_html:
When a metal sheet of thickness ( $\frac{2d}{3}$ ) is introduced between the plates of a capacitor, it divides the capacitor into two separate capacitors. The metal sheet acts as a new plate in each capacitor, and because the metal is a conductor, it is at the same potential as the plates on either side.

The capacitance of the original capacitor with air between the plates is given by:

$C_{1}=\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{d}$

where ( $\epsilon_{0}$ ) is the permittivity of free space, ( $A$ ) is the area of one of the plates, and ( $d$ ) is the distance between the plates.

When the metal sheet of thickness ( $\frac{2d}{3}$ ) is introduced, the distance between the plates is reduced by ( $\frac{2d}{3}$ ), so the capacitance of each of the new capacitors is:

$C^{'}=\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{d-\frac{2d}{3}}$

Simplifying, we get:

$C^{'}=\frac{3\epsilon_{0}A}{d}$

Since the two capacitors are in parallel with each other, the total capacitance is:

$C_{2}=2C^{'}=2 \times \frac{3\epsilon_{0}A}{d}=3C_{1}$

So the ratio of the capacitances is:

$\frac{C_{2}}{C_{1}}=3:1$

$\Rightarrow C_{s}=\frac{C}{2}$

When both capacitors are connected in parallel, their equivalent capacitance will be

Cp = C + C = 2C

$\therefore$ The ratio of equivalent capacitance in series and parallel combination is

$\frac{C_{s}}{C_{p}}=\frac{C/2}{2C}=\frac{1}{4}$

$\therefore$ Cs : Cp = 1 : 4

questions.explanation_text: Area = 100 m 2 Separation (d) = 10 m Thickness = 5 m Dielectric constant (K) = 10 $c_{1}=\frac{KA\epsilon_{0}}{d},c_{2}=\frac{A\epsilon_{0}}{d}$ $\Rightarrow$ $c_{eq}=\frac{c_{1}c_{2}}{c_{1}+c_{2}}=\frac{\frac{KA\epsilon_{0}}{d} \times \frac{A\epsilon_{0}}{d}}{\frac{KA\epsilon_{0}}{d}+\frac{A\epsilon_{0}}{d}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $c_{eq}=\frac{KA^{2}\epsilon_{0}^{2}}{d^{2}} \times \frac{d}{A\epsilon_{0}(1+K)}$ $\Rightarrow$ $c_{eq}=\frac{KA\epsilon_{0}}{d(1+K)}=\frac{10 \times 100 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}}{5(1+10)}$ $\Rightarrow$ $c_{eq}=\frac{8.85 \times 10^{-9}}{55}=0.1609090 \times 10^{-9}$ $\Rightarrow$ $C_{eq}=160.90 \times 10^{-12}$ $\Rightarrow$ $C_{eq}=161$ PF

Thickness = 5 m

$c_{1}=\frac{KA\epsilon_{0}}{d},c_{2}=\frac{A\epsilon_{0}}{d}$

$\Rightarrow$ $c_{eq}=\frac{c_{1}c_{2}}{c_{1}+c_{2}}=\frac{\frac{KA\epsilon_{0}}{d} \times \frac{A\epsilon_{0}}{d}}{\frac{KA\epsilon_{0}}{d}+\frac{A\epsilon_{0}}{d}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $C_{eq}=160.90 \times 10^{-12}$

is connected to a battery of emf V. A dielectric

questions.question_html: A parallel plate capacitor has plate of length 'l', width ‘w’ and separation of plates is ‘d’. It is connected to a battery of emf V. A dielectric slab of the same thickness ‘d’ and of dielectric constant k = 4 is being inserted between the plates of the capacitor. At what length of the slab inside plates, will the energy stored in the capacitor be two times the initial energy stored?
questions.explanation_text: C i = $\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{d}=\frac{\epsilon_{0}lw}{d}$ U i = $\frac{1}{2}C_{i}V^{2}$ = $\frac{1}{2}\frac{\epsilon_{0}lw}{d}V^{2}$ C f = C 1 + C 2 = $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}A_{1}}{d}+\frac{\epsilon_{0}A_{2}}{d}$ = $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}wx}{d}+\frac{\epsilon_{0}w(l-x)}{d}$ = $\frac{\epsilon_{0}w}{d}[Kx+l-x]$ $\therefore$ U f = $\frac{1}{2}C_{f}V^{2}$ = $\frac{1}{2}\frac{\epsilon_{0}w}{d}[Kx+l-x]V^{2}$ Given U f = 2U i $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{2}\frac{\epsilon_{0}w}{d}[Kx+l-x]V^{2}$ = 2 $\times$ $\frac{1}{2}\frac{\epsilon_{0}lw}{d}V^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ kx + l – x = 2 l $\Rightarrow$ 4x – x = l $\Rightarrow$ 3x = l $\Rightarrow$ x = $\frac{l}{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
Ci = $\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{d}=\frac{\epsilon_{0}lw}{d}$

Ui = $\frac{1}{2}C_{i}V^{2}$ = $\frac{1}{2}\frac{\epsilon_{0}lw}{d}V^{2}$

Cf = C1 + C2

= $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}A_{1}}{d}+\frac{\epsilon_{0}A_{2}}{d}$

= $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}wx}{d}+\frac{\epsilon_{0}w(l-x)}{d}$

= $\frac{\epsilon_{0}w}{d}[Kx+l-x]$

$\therefore$ Uf = $\frac{1}{2}C_{f}V^{2}$

= $\frac{1}{2}\frac{\epsilon_{0}w}{d}[Kx+l-x]V^{2}$

Given Uf = 2Ui

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{2}\frac{\epsilon_{0}w}{d}[Kx+l-x]V^{2}$ = 2 $\times$ $\frac{1}{2}\frac{\epsilon_{0}lw}{d}V^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ kx + l – x = 2l

$\Rightarrow$ 4x – x = l

$\Rightarrow$ 3x = l

$\Rightarrow$ x = $\frac{l}{3}$

$=C_{12}+C_{34}$

$C_{12}=\frac{\frac{K_{1}\epsilon_{0}L^{2}}{d} \times \frac{K_{2}\epsilon_{0}L^{2}}{d}}{\frac{K_{1}\epsilon_{0}L^{2}}{d}+\frac{K_{2}\epsilon_{0}L^{2}}{d}}$

questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor is made of two square plates of side 'a', separated by a distance d (d < < a). The lower triangular portion is filled with a dielectric of dielectric constant K, as shown in the figure. Capacitance of this capacitor is :
questions.question_html: A parallel plate capacitor is made of two square plates of side 'a', separated by a distance d (d < < a). The lower triangular portion is filled with a dielectric of dielectric constant K, as shown in the figure. Capacitance of this capacitor is :
questions.explanation_text: Let the capacitance of the upper part of the strip of length dx is dC 1 and lower part of the strip is dC 2 $\therefore$ dC 1 = $\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{d-y}$ and dC 2 = $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}adx}{y}$ Here dC 1 and dC 2 are in series. So, equivalent capacitance, $\frac{1}{dC}$ = $\frac{1}{dC_{1}}+\frac{1}{dC_{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{dC}$ = $\frac{d-y}{\epsilon_{0}adx}+\frac{y}{\epsilon_{0}Kadx}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{dC}$ = $\frac{1}{\epsilon_{0}adx}$ ( d $-$ y + $\frac{y}{K}$ ) $\Rightarrow$ dC = $\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{(d-y)+\frac{y}{K}}$ We can divide entire parallel plate capacitor into similar part like the strip of length dx and all the strips will have common end A and B. So they are in parallel. So equivalent capacitance is the sum of all the strips capacitance. $\therefore$ $\int dC$ = $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{(d-y)+\frac{y}{K}}$ $\Rightarrow$ C = $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{(d-y)+\frac{y}{K}}$ From above diagram you can find this $\rightarrow$ tan $\theta$ = $\frac{y}{x}$ Also tan $\theta$ = $\frac{d}{a}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{y}{x}$ = $\frac{d}{a}$ $\Rightarrow$ y = $\frac{d}{a}$ x By putting this value of y in the integration we get, C = $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{d-\frac{d}{a}x+\frac{d}{Ka}x}$ = $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{d+(\frac{1}{K}-1)\frac{d}{a}x}$ = $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\epsilon_{0}a^{2}dx}{da+(\frac{1-K}{K})xd}$ = $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}dx}{Kda+(1-K)xd}$ = $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}}{d(1-k)}[ln((1-K)x+Ka)]_{0}^{a}$ = $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}}{d(1-k)}[ln(a)-ln(Ka)]$ = $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}}{d(1-k)}ln(\frac{a}{Ka})$ = $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}}{d(1-k)}ln(\frac{1}{K})$ = $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}}{d(1-k)}ln(K)$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the capacitance of the upper part of the strip of length dx is dC1 and lower part of the strip is dC2

$\therefore$    dC1 = $\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{d-y}$

and dC2 = $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}adx}{y}$

Here dC1 and dC2 are in series.

So, equivalent capacitance,

$\frac{1}{dC}$ = $\frac{1}{dC_{1}}+\frac{1}{dC_{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$     $\frac{1}{dC}$ = $\frac{d-y}{\epsilon_{0}adx}+\frac{y}{\epsilon_{0}Kadx}$

$\Rightarrow$     $\frac{1}{dC}$ = $\frac{1}{\epsilon_{0}adx}$ ( d $-$ y + $\frac{y}{K}$ )

$\Rightarrow$    dC = $\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{(d-y)+\frac{y}{K}}$

We can divide entire parallel plate capacitor into similar part like the strip of length dx and all the strips will have common end A and B. So they are in parallel.

So equivalent capacitance is the sum of all the strips capacitance.

$\therefore$     $\int dC$ = $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{(d-y)+\frac{y}{K}}$

$\Rightarrow$    C = $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{(d-y)+\frac{y}{K}}$

From above diagram you can find this $\rightarrow$



tan $\theta$ = $\frac{y}{x}$

Also tan $\theta$ = $\frac{d}{a}$

$\therefore$     $\frac{y}{x}$ = $\frac{d}{a}$

$\Rightarrow$    y = $\frac{d}{a}$ x

By putting this value of y in the integration we get,

C = $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{d-\frac{d}{a}x+\frac{d}{Ka}x}$

= $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\epsilon_{0}adx}{d+(\frac{1}{K}-1)\frac{d}{a}x}$

= $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\epsilon_{0}a^{2}dx}{da+(\frac{1-K}{K})xd}$

= $\int_{0}^{a}\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}dx}{Kda+(1-K)xd}$

= $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}}{d(1-k)}[ln((1-K)x+Ka)]_{0}^{a}$

= $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}}{d(1-k)}[ln(a)-ln(Ka)]$

= $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}}{d(1-k)}ln(\frac{a}{Ka})$

= $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}}{d(1-k)}ln(\frac{1}{K})$

= $\frac{K\epsilon_{0}a^{2}}{d(1-k)}ln(K)$

questions.question_text: A capacitor C 1 = 1.0 $\mu$ F is charged up to a voltage V = 60 V by connecting it to battery B through switch (1). Now C 1 is disconnected from battery and connected to a circuit consisting of two uncharged capacitors $C_{2}=3.0\mu F$ and C 3 = 6.0 $\mu$ F through switch (2), as shown in the figure. The sum of final charges on C 2 and C 3 is :
questions.question_html: A capacitor C1 = 1.0 $\mu$ F is charged up to a voltage V = 60 V by connecting it to battery B through switch (1). Now C1 is disconnected from battery and connected to a circuit consisting of two uncharged capacitors $C_{2}=3.0\mu F$ and C3 = 6.0 $\mu$ F through switch (2), as shown in the figure. The sum of final charges on C2 and C3 is :
questions.explanation_text: Given : C 1 = 1.0 $\mu$ F; C 2 = 3.0 $\mu$ F; C 3 = 6.0 $\mu$ F Capacitance C 2 and C 3 are in series, their equivalent capacitance is $\frac{1}{C}=\frac{1}{C_{2}}+\frac{1}{C_{3}} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{C}=\frac{C_{2}+C_{3}}{C_{2}C_{3}}$ $\Rightarrow C=\frac{C_{2}C_{3}}{C_{2}+C_{3}}=\frac{3.0\mu F \times 6.0\mu F}{3.0\mu F+6.0\mu F}=2\mu F$ Charge on C 1 when battery is connected to switch (1) is $=C_{1} \times 60$ ..... (1) Charge when battery is connected to switch (2) is $=(C_{1}+C)V^{'}$ ...... (2) Equating Eq. (1) and (2), we get $(C_{1}+C)V^{'}=60C_{1} \Rightarrow V^{'}=\frac{60C_{1}}{C_{1}+C}$ $\Rightarrow V^{'}=\frac{60 \times 1\mu F}{1\mu F+2\mu F}=\frac{60 \times 1\mu F}{3\mu F}=20V$ Final charge on C 2 and C 3 is $Q=CV^{'}=2\mu F \times 20=40\mu C$ Therefore, $Q=40\mu C$
questions.explanation_html:
Given : C1 = 1.0 $\mu$ F; C2 = 3.0 $\mu$ F; C3 = 6.0 $\mu$ F

Capacitance C2 and C3 are in series, their equivalent capacitance is

$\frac{1}{C}=\frac{1}{C_{2}}+\frac{1}{C_{3}} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{C}=\frac{C_{2}+C_{3}}{C_{2}C_{3}}$

$\Rightarrow C=\frac{C_{2}C_{3}}{C_{2}+C_{3}}=\frac{3.0\mu F \times 6.0\mu F}{3.0\mu F+6.0\mu F}=2\mu F$

Charge on C1 when battery is connected to switch (1) is

$=C_{1} \times 60$ ..... (1)

Charge when battery is connected to switch (2) is

$=(C_{1}+C)V^{'}$ ...... (2)

Equating Eq. (1) and (2), we get

$(C_{1}+C)V^{'}=60C_{1} \Rightarrow V^{'}=\frac{60C_{1}}{C_{1}+C}$

$\Rightarrow V^{'}=\frac{60 \times 1\mu F}{1\mu F+2\mu F}=\frac{60 \times 1\mu F}{3\mu F}=20V$

Final charge on C2 and C3 is $Q=CV^{'}=2\mu F \times 20=40\mu C$

Therefore, $Q=40\mu C$

questions.question_html:
A combination of parallel plate capacitors is maintained at a certain potential difference.



When a 3 mm thick slab is introduced between all the plates, in order to maintain the same potential difference, the distance between the plates is increased by 2.4 mm. Find the dielectric constant of the slab.
questions.explanation_text: Before introducing the slab between the plates of all three capacitors, we have $C_{1}=\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{3}$ After introducing the slab between the plates of all three capacitors, we have $C_{1}=K\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{3}+\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{2.4}$ As the capacitors are in series, we get $\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{3}=\frac{(\frac{K\epsilon_{0}A}{3}).(\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{2.4})}{(\frac{K\epsilon_{0}A}{3})+(\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{2.4})}$ Therefore, the dielectric constant of the slab is $\Rightarrow 3K=2.4K+3$ $\Rightarrow 0.6K=3$ $\Rightarrow K=\frac{3}{0.6}=\frac{30}{6}=5$
questions.explanation_html:
Before introducing the slab between the plates of all three capacitors, we have

$C_{1}=\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{3}$

After introducing the slab between the plates of all three capacitors, we have

$C_{1}=K\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{3}+\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{2.4}$

As the capacitors are in series, we get

$\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{3}=\frac{(\frac{K\epsilon_{0}A}{3}).(\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{2.4})}{(\frac{K\epsilon_{0}A}{3})+(\frac{\epsilon_{0}A}{2.4})}$

Therefore, the dielectric constant of the slab is

$\Rightarrow 3K=2.4K+3$

$\Rightarrow 0.6K=3$

$\Rightarrow K=\frac{3}{0.6}=\frac{30}{6}=5$

questions.explanation_text: Initial energy of capacitor, $E_{1}=\frac{q_{1}^{2}}{2C}$ Final energy of capacitor, $E_{2}=\frac{1}{2}E_{1}=\frac{q_{1}^{2}}{4C}=(\frac{\frac{q_{1}}{\sqrt{2}}}{2C})^{2}$ $\therefore$ $t_{1}=$ time for the charge to reduce to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ of its initial value and $t_{2}=$ time for the charge to reduce to $\frac{1}{4}$ of its initial value We have, $q_{2}=q_{1}e^{-t/CR}$ $\Rightarrow ln(\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}})=-\frac{t}{CR}$ $\therefore$ $ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{-t_{1}}{CR}...(1)$ and $ln(\frac{1}{4})=\frac{-t_{2}}{CR}...(2)$ By $(1)$ and $(2),$ $\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\frac{ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}{ln(\frac{1}{4})}$ $=\frac{1}{2}\frac{ln(\frac{1}{2})}{2ln(\frac{1}{2})}=\frac{1}{4}$
questions.explanation_html:
Initial energy of capacitor, $E_{1}=\frac{q_{1}^{2}}{2C}$

Final energy of capacitor, $E_{2}=\frac{1}{2}E_{1}=\frac{q_{1}^{2}}{4C}=(\frac{\frac{q_{1}}{\sqrt{2}}}{2C})^{2}$

$\therefore$ $t_{1}=$ time for the charge to reduce to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ of its initial value

and $t_{2}=$ time for the charge to reduce to $\frac{1}{4}$ of its initial value

We have, $q_{2}=q_{1}e^{-t/CR}$

$\Rightarrow ln(\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}})=-\frac{t}{CR}$

$\therefore$ $ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{-t_{1}}{CR}...(1)$

and $ln(\frac{1}{4})=\frac{-t_{2}}{CR}...(2)$

By $(1)$ and $(2),$ $\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\frac{ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}{ln(\frac{1}{4})}$

$=\frac{1}{2}\frac{ln(\frac{1}{2})}{2ln(\frac{1}{2})}=\frac{1}{4}$

The dielectric slab is slowly removed from between the plates and then reinserted. The net work done by the system in this process is
questions.question_html: A parallel plate condenser with a dielectric of dielectric constant $K$ between the plates has a capacity $C$ and is charged to a potential $V$ volt. The dielectric slab is slowly removed from between the plates and then reinserted. The net work done by the system in this process is
questions.explanation_text: First, let's consider the capacitor with the dielectric between its plates. The charge on the capacitor is Q, its capacitance is C (which includes the effect of the dielectric), and the potential difference (voltage) across its plates is V. According to the formula for the energy stored in a capacitor : $U=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$ we find that the energy is equal to half of the product of the capacitance and the square of the voltage. Now, consider the process where the dielectric slab is removed from the capacitor. When the dielectric is removed, the capacitance of the capacitor decreases. However, because the capacitor is not connected to anything that can supply or absorb charge, the charge Q on the capacitor stays the same. Since the charge stays the same but the capacitance decreases, the voltage V across the capacitor must increase to keep Q = CV true. The energy of the capacitor without the dielectric is still given by : $U=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$ but now C is smaller and V is larger. However, because both C and V 2 change in such a way that their product remains constant, the energy of the capacitor doesn't change when the dielectric is removed. Therefore, the energy of the capacitor before the dielectric is removed is the same as the energy of the capacitor after the dielectric is removed. When the dielectric is reinserted, the process is just reversed, so again no net work is done. So the total work done by the system in the process of removing the dielectric and then reinserting it is zero. This is because work is the transfer of energy, and in this case, the energy of the system (the charged capacitor) does not change. Therefore, no energy is transferred, so no work is done.

So the total work done by the system in the process of removing the dielectric and then reinserting it is zero. This is because work is the transfer of energy, and in this case, the energy of the system (the charged capacitor) does not change. Therefore, no energy is transferred, so no work is done.

The equivalent capacitance of $n$ identical capacitors of capacitance $C$ is equal to $nC.$ Energy stored in this capacitor

$E=\frac{1}{2}(nC)V^{2}=\frac{1}{2}nCV^{2}$
